svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 1. The only line in the ranking that changes the attacker's job
svg.desc: A ranking of authentication methods split by a single dividing line rather than by tiers. Above the line are hardware security keys and passkeys with user verification, which share one property: a perfect replica of a login page obtains nothing usable. Below the line are time based codes from an application, push approval with number matching, plain push approval, and codes by text message. All four share the same defeat, which is that the value can be relayed by an attacker in real time, and they are ranked by how many additional ways there are to lose them. A band below notes that email codes and security questions are not second factors at all.
svg.text: Figure 1: The Only Line That Changes the Attacker's Job
A five star method and a four star method sound one step apart. They are not one step apart, and the star rating is what hides that.
A perfect replica of the login page obtains nothing it can use. Not because you noticed, and not because you were careful.

svg.text: EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE SHARES ONE DEFEAT
You hand over a value, and an attacker relays it to the real site while it is still valid. Ranked below by what else can go wrong.

svg.text: Two things commonly offered as a second factor are not a second factor at all

g.text: Codes to your email address. The same channel your account recovery already uses, so it protects nothing your email does not already protect. For an email account it is circular.
Security questions. Still something you know, so not a second category at all, and the answers are frequently published by you. Use invented answers stored in the vault.

svg.text: Getting above the line is one decision. Rearranging methods below it is housekeeping, and worth doing, and not the same thing.
